sections.name: The expensive part of origination is not the list.

items.text: What origination costs · What it means
The expensive part of origination is not the list.
Where the time goes

Origination in a vertical is a sequence: map the sector, find the owners, reach them, qualify the ones who answer, and build enough of a relationship that a conversation about selling is possible. An associate doing that work full time cannot run a live process at the same time, and the sector knowledge that makes the work efficient takes a year or more to build: which names are unbuyable and why, which owners have already said no to three other buyers, which companies are owned by a platform that will never sell. A new hire adds those names to the list again.

The second cost is the one nobody budgets: the letter that dies. A buyer under exclusivity has stopped looking at other deals, has committed diligence invoices, and has spent the owner’s patience. The published averages run from 37 days where a family office was the buyer to 159 where a senior lender was, and the independent sponsor, who raises the equity after signing, holds the letter longest of all.
The expensive part of origination is not the list. It is the year it takes to know what is on it, and the months lost when a letter dies.

What the calculator does

It multiplies the associate’s compensation by the months each signed letter takes, adds the days under exclusivity for a letter that dies, and multiplies by the number of letters that died last year. It does not include diligence invoices, legal fees or anyone’s time but the associate’s, so the result is a floor. The companion calculator on the deal coverage page estimates the share of your own market your firm sees.
